source_text:
{Hebr 1,3} ∆όξαν μὲν εὐφήμως κέκληκε
τὸν πατέρα, ἀπαύγασμα δὲ τὸν υἱόν, διδάσκων ἐκ παραδείγματος ἐκ πατρός τε αὐτὸν
εἶναι καὶ συναΐδιον τῷ πατρί· τοιοῦτον γὰρ τὸ ἀπαύγασμα ἐκ τοῦ ἡλίου τε ὂν καὶ
συνυπάρχον αὐτῷ. οὐκοῦν ἂν ἥλιον εἴποι τις οὔποτε τοῦ οἰκείου πρεσβύτερον
ἀπαυγάσματος. ἔφη δὲ αὐτὸ δίχα τῆς πατρὸς συλλαβῆς κατὰ τὸ ἰδίωμα τῆς γραφῆς.
{Hebr 5,8} Ἀντὶ τοῦ τῷ πάθει τὸ μάθημα τῆς ὑπακοῆς ἔχων ἐντελέστατον
ἐπεδείξατο, καὶ ταῦτα τυγχάνων υἱός. οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς λέγειν εἰώθαμεν.
thought_title: The Son as radiance and the lesson of obedience
orientation: The author is explaining Hebrews 1:3 and 5:8, showing how the Son is called radiance to teach his coeternity with the Father, and how Christ's suffering displayed the lesson of obedience.
pass_a_gloss: Glory he has called the Father in a reverent way, and radiance the Son, teaching from an example that he is from the Father and coeternal with the Father; for such is the radiance, being from the sun and coexisting with it. Therefore one would never say the sun is older than its own radiance. He said it apart from the syllable 'patr-' according to the idiom of Scripture. Instead of: having the lesson of obedience through suffering most perfectly he displayed it, and this while being Son. Thus also we are accustomed to say.

choices.why: The adverb describes calling the Father 'glory' with fitting reverence, not merely 'well' or 'auspiciously'.
Glossary term for the Son's relation to the Father; 'radiance' is the fixed rendering.
The point of the sun example is that radiance is not younger than its source; 'coeternal' captures the theological claim.
The author notes Hebrews says 'radiance' without adding 'of the Father,' following Scripture's idiom; the literal phrase is kept.

choices.term: τῷ πάθει τὸ μάθημα τῆς ὑπακοῆς ἔχων
choices.english: having the lesson of obedience through suffering
choices.why: The dative τῷ πάθει is instrumental, and the participle ἔχων is kept as 'having' to preserve the construction being explained.
rejected: learning obedience from what he suffered

choices.why: The superlative adverb and middle verb show Christ demonstrated the lesson completely; 'displayed' keeps the demonstrative force.

bible_refs.note: τῷ πάθει τὸ μάθημα τῆς ὑπακοῆς

pass_b_english: He calls the Father “glory” in a reverent way, and the Son “radiance,” teaching by this example that the Son is from the Father and coeternal with the Father. For radiance is like that: it comes from the sun and coexists with it. So no one could ever say that the sun is older than its own radiance. And he said this without the syllable “Father,” following the idiom of Scripture.

In place of “Though he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered,” it means that through suffering he had the lesson of obedience and displayed it most perfectly, even though he was Son. We too are accustomed to speak this way.

problems.why: δίχα means 'apart from/separate from,' not 'without' in sense of lacking; 'father' is genitive of πατήρ, but context suggests 'apart from the syllable patr-'.
problems.fix: apart from the syllable 'patr-,' following the idiom of Scripture

problems.why: English adds 'This means that' hiding that author quotes Hebrews 5:8.
problems.fix: In place of 'Though he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered,' it means that through suffering...
problems.ruling: Ἀντὶ τοῦ means 'instead of'; 'This means that' misrepresents the connection and obscures the Hebrews 5:8 quotation.

edits.old: And he said this without the syllable “father,” following the idiom of Scripture.
edits.new: And he said this apart from the syllable “patr-,” following the idiom of Scripture.

edits.old: This means that through suffering he had the lesson of obedience and displayed it most perfectly, even though he was Son.
edits.new: In place of “Though he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered,” it means that through suffering he had the lesson of obedience and displayed it most perfectly, even though he was Son.

problems.why: συλλαβῆς here means 'conjunction/comprehension' (from συλλαμβάνω), not 'syllable'; he said it without mentioning the Father directly.
problems.fix: without explicit mention of the Father
problems.ruling: συλλαβῆς here means 'mention/comprehension' (συλλαμβάνω), not 'syllable'; 'apart from the syllable patr-' misleads readers.

edits.old: And he said this apart from the syllable “patr-,” following the idiom of Scripture.
edits.new: And he said this without explicit mention of the Father, following the idiom of Scripture.

problems.quote: without explicit mention of the Father
problems.why: συλλαβῆς means 'syllable,' i.e., the word 'Father'; not 'explicit mention' generally.

edits.old: And he said this without explicit mention of the Father, following the idiom of Scripture.
edits.new: And he said this without the syllable “Father,” following the idiom of Scripture.

last_rejected.quote: He calls the Father “glory” in a reverent way
last_rejected.source_quote: Δόξαν μὲν εὐφήμως κέκληκε τὸν πατέρα
last_rejected.why: εὐφήμως means 'with good report/praise' or 'auspiciously,' not 'in a reverent way'; the point is he calls the Father 'Glory' euphemistically/figuratively, not reverently.
last_rejected.fix: He calls the Father 'Glory' by a gracious title
last_rejected.ruling: εὐφήμως can mean 'reverently'; rendering within normal range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: through suffering he had the lesson of obedience and displayed it most perfectly
last_rejected.source_quote: τῷ πάθει τὸ μάθημα τῆς ὑπακοῆς ἔχων ἐντελέστατον ἐπεδείξατο
last_rejected.why: ἔχων is causal/attendant circumstance: 'having learned' or 'by having,' not 'he had'; the Greek says he displayed the lesson most perfectly, not that he 'had' it then displayed it.
last_rejected.fix: through suffering, having learned the lesson of obedience, he displayed it most perfectly
last_rejected.ruling: ἔχων rendered 'had' is within range; 'displayed it most perfectly' correctly renders ἐπεδείξατο ἐντελέστατον.
